In parallel, we are developing a bilayer film by combining purified PLL with chitosan and sodium alginate-based materials. Our goal is to create a cling film that is both antimicrobial and biodegradable, offering a safer and more sustainable alternative to traditional plastic packaging.

title: LL-37 — the Human Antimicrobial Peptide​
text: LL-37 — the Human Antimicrobial Peptide​. Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a severe global public health threat, with drug-resistant bacteria increasingly endangering human health.The human antimicrobial peptide LL-37 offers a promising solution due to its high safety, low resistance potential, and immunomodulatory activity. Our project employs Saccharomyces cerevisiae as a chassis cell, integrating genetic engineering, fermentation optimization, and a D2P cell-free system to achieve high-yield biosynthesis of functional LL-37 at a significantly lower cost than chemical synthesis.We developed the CytoFlow platform, integrating biodynamic simulations, reinforcement learning, and diffusion models. This platform optimizes S. cerevisiae cultivation and designs LL-37 variants with superior antimicrobial performance. We also developed the EFUV-Cycle and RLAI-Cycle, and designed the educational game Cytopia Defense, the "Life Glow" bio-art activity, and the handbook Busting Rumors about Synthetic Biology to enhance the project's impact in both Integrated Human Practices and education.

title: RSAV-Recombinat Scorpion Antivenom
text: RSAV-Recombinat Scorpion Antivenom. Envenomation by venomous animals remains a global health concern, with scorpionism being particularly critical in Mexico, causing around 300,000 stings and around 1,400 deaths each year. Our project proposes an integrated three-system approach to address this issue. First, we aim to develop microbial production systems for recombinant antivenoms as sustainable and ethical alternatives to animal-derived ones. Second, we implement educational and social strategies to promote prevention and awareness within vulnerable communities. Third, we apply data modeling and optimization tools to improve healthcare logistics and accessibility in marginalized regions. Experimentally, we constructed an expression vector using the pPICZα backbone under AOX1 promoter control for expression in the Komagataella phaffii strain OPENPichia pep4 yps1. Alongside, our outreach and modeling efforts connect synthetic biology and community engagement, working toward a future where preventable deaths from scorpionism in Mexico are reduced as much as possible.

title: SnaPFAS
text: SnaPFAS. Perfluoroalkyl and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) contamination is a global concern due to their persistence in water, widespread presence in daily life, and long-term health risks. Among them, perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) is the most prevalent and hazardous pollutant. By developing an integrated PFOA & fluoride ions biosensor, optimizing PFOA-degrading enzymes, and designing a systematic hardware platform, we aim to establish a PFOA governance system that integrates detection, biodegradation, and safe processing, providing a practical solution to mitigate environmental and health impacts.

title: Project SeQUESTer: Engineering a Yeast-Based Biosystem for Toxic Heavy Metal Detection and Removal
text: Project SeQUESTer: Engineering a Yeast-Based Biosystem for Toxic Heavy Metal Detection and Removal. Project SeQUESTer aims to develop a sustainable, bioengineered filtration system to combat toxic heavy metal (THM) contamination in water, with an initial focus on lead (Pb). Lead pollution arises from industrial activity and aging infrastructure, posing persistent health and environmental hazards, especially in under-resourced communities. SeQUESTer introduces an innovative genetic sensing and sequestration platform using Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Our system integrates a riboswitch that detects lead ions, a reversible genetic memory switch that records exposure events, with the future direction to incorporate metal transporters that enhance cellular uptake and immobilization of lead. These engineered yeast cells are embedded within a porous agarose–zeolite scaffold housed in a scalable, modular biofiltration unit. This design enables simultaneous detection and removal of lead while maintaining environmental safety. SeQUESTer provides a low-cost, accessible, and eco-conscious alternative to conventional water treatment technologies.

title: LANCET: A novel diagnostic and therapeutic combating Lyme Disease
text: LANCET: A novel diagnostic and therapeutic combating Lyme Disease. 89,000 cases of Lyme disease were reported to the CDC in 2023, yet experts estimate that nearly half-a-million Americans are infected with Borrelia burgdorferi annually. This significant underdiagnosis is due to the rapid dissemination of the bacteria into tissue, causing current tests to rely on antibodies produced weeks post-infection. However, the outer surface protein, CspZ, persists in the bloodstream, allowing for early detection through LANCET. Our diagnostic workflow begins with proximity-dependent ligation to detect CspZ and produce DNA, which is then amplified by recombinase polymerase amplification. Cas12a targets this DNA, providing a user-friendly output through a lateral flow assay. Even with improved diagnosis, treatment continues to rely on antibiotics, contributing to antimicrobial resistance and failing to address post-treatment Lyme disease. LANCET offers a novel approach through a multiplexed CRISPR-interference system to silence critical genes, effectively killing the bacteria. Our initiative also includes community education, fostering proactive behaviors against Lyme.

title: Filaggrin: an alternative solution for eczema
text: Filaggrin: an alternative solution for eczema. Atopic Dermatitis (eczema) stems largely from filaggrin (FLG) mutations, causing skin barrier failure. Current treatments only manage inflammation. We propose synthesizing artificial FLG to directly repair the barrier, delivered via jojoba oil for optimal topical application. This targets the condition's root cause, the skin barrier dysfunction.

title: ArMOLDgeddon, Safe and Efficient Mold Eliminator
text: ArMOLDgeddon, Safe and Efficient Mold Eliminator. Accounting for up to 20% of all respiratory allergy cases in humid areas, reaching a pervalence of around 30% in many countries around the world, indoors mold problem comprises one of the most serious threat to public health. To tackle this risk, GreatBay-SCIE 2025 devised a brand new mold killer, ArMOLDgeddon. Harnessing the antifungal properties of enzymes chitinase, glucanase, lysozyme and monoterpenoid geraniol, ArMOLDgeddon provides a safe and effective alternative to current mold removers. Chitinase and glucanase degrade critical structural polymers of the mold cell wall, while lysozyme magnifies the damage through cationic interaction with the cell wall components and disruption of fungal membranes. Geraniol, apart from furthering the attack on fungal membrane, provides a pleasant fragrance.  Furthermore, with the help of artificial intelligence and strong carbohydrate binding domains, ArMOLDgeddon evolves and improves, expediting towards the goal of the annihilation of mold-related diseases, and eradicating this pervasive global health threat.

title: QURES: Quorum-sensing Utilizing Reprogrammed Engineered Symbionts for Atopic Dermatitis
text: QURES: Quorum-sensing Utilizing Reprogrammed Engineered Symbionts for Atopic Dermatitis. As the incidence of atopic dermatitis is increasing, the poor therapeutic experience of patients relying on long-term steroid use and immunosuppressants requires a breakthrough. Current treatments face a high recurrence rate. We stand to develop a more favorable treatment experience. Relevant studies have shown that the microbiome plays a critical role in the pathogenesis of atopic dermatitis, particularly the presence of Staphylococcus aureus and its inflammatory effects. Based on this, we designed a therapeutic system using engineered Staphylococcus epidermidis. We genetically modified Staphylococcus epidermidis to sense the AIP-C secreted by S. aureus and activate two downstream therapeutic pathways. The first pathway produces an nanobody that targets and neutralizes the inflammatory cytokine, while the second secretes AIP-C to suppress the virulence of S. aureus. Together, our system offers a safe and long-lasting therapeutic strategy, representing a paradigm shift in atopic dermatitis management - moving from symptom suppression to microbiome-mediated disease prevention.

title: SOLARIS
text: SOLARIS. Billions of years ago, cyanobacteria transformed Earth’s atmosphere through carbon fixation, enabling the metabolic foundation of modern ecosystems. Yet, despite its central role, photosynthetic carbon fixation has not changed much since its origin. With SOLARIS, we reexamine this long-standing process from the perspective of synthetic biology, foundationally changing and advancing CO₂ fixation in cyanobacteria. Our solution lays the groundwork for photosynthesis 2.0 to overcome the kinetic and oxygen-sensitivity limitations of RuBisCO by introducing a distinct carbon fixation cycle supported by a carbonic anhydrase system we newly identified and confirmed for activity. This has the potential to make cyanobacteria far better at fixing CO₂ from the atmosphere and turning it into biomass. SOLARIS offers the tools and methodologies for rewriting core metabolic pathways with synthetic biology for optimizing synthetic carbon fixation cycles in vivo and in vitro, a foundational step toward programmable photosynthesis and a new generation of engineered phototrophs.

title: Clotho: Weaving a Cure for PDAC
text: Clotho: Weaving a Cure for PDAC. Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC) causes nearly half a million deaths worldwide each year, with incidence and mortality rates almost identical, reflecting the lack of effective treatments. To address this, we developed Clotho, a modular gene therapy designed to cure PDAC. Using an adeno-associated virus, we deliver a therapeutic transgene that activates exclusively in cancer cells. Once inside, it produces circular RNAs and the enzyme Cytosine Deaminase. The circular RNAs act as sponges for tumor-promoting miRNAs, enhancing cancer cell sensitivity to treatment. Meanwhile, the enzyme converts the harmless prodrug 5-fluorocytosine into the toxic compound 5-fluorouracil, selectively killing malignant cells. Complementing this, our software platform Kathesis generates patient-specific circular RNA sequences based on individual genetic profiles. This dual approach enables precise, personalized, and targeted therapy, reducing off-target effects and introducing a novel strategy to overcome drug resistance in PDAC and potentially other diseases.

title: Plants vs. PET: Combatting Microplastic Pollution with Plant-Based PETase
text: Plants vs. PET: Combatting Microplastic Pollution with Plant-Based PETase. Thailand ranked sixth in the world for mismanaged plastic waste, sending over a million tonnes into the oceans each year (Labcom et al., 2024). Microplastics are now found throughout the country’s ecosystems—from marine animals to water, air, and farmland—threatening wildlife, food safety, and human health (Chanpiwat, 2021). The most common culprit is polyethylene terephthalate (PET), making up 37% of poorly managed waste. In 2016, scientists discovered PETase, an enzyme from Ideonella sakaiensis that can break down PET. However, such microbial hosts are inefficient, unsafe, and unsustainable. Therefore, the Thailand‑RIS iGEM 2025 team explored a different approach—producing PETase in plants—of which we present the first successful demonstration. Although stable transformation is still underway, we achieved transient expression of PETase fused with an alpha‑amylase 3S signal peptide in Nicotiana benthamiana, resulting in extracellular secretion. This proof of concept lays the groundwork for scalable, sustainable plant-based strategies against forever-increasing plastic pollution.

title: CML2-Powered: A Niche-Adaptive Biosensor for Precise Arsenic Detection in Rice Paddies
text: CML2-Powered: A Niche-Adaptive Biosensor for Precise Arsenic Detection in Rice Paddies. Arsenic contamination in rice paddies threatens food safety and environmental health. Traditional large-instrument-based monitoring is costly and unsuitable for on-site rapid screening. To solve this, our project develops a novel arsenic biosensor via the "niche-matching" principle, sourcing key elements from Cupriavidus metallidurans CML2 (a rice endophyte adapted to paddies). We construct an "AND-gate-like" genetic circuit with a split-GFP system to reduce basal leakage and boost signal-to-noise ratio, and optimize performance through multiple "Design-Build-Test-Learn" (DBTL) cycles for sensitive, specific arsenic detection. This biosensor enables on-site paddy arsenic monitoring and lays a foundation for future "detection-remediation" microbial agents, aiding sustainable agriculture and environmental protection.

title: SKIPPIT: Harnessing the power of RNA to unlock translational-level control.
text: SKIPPIT: Harnessing the power of RNA to unlock translational-level control.. As synthetic biology positions itself as a field of the future, the need for new tools that allow better control of protein expression and new options for genetic engineering is clear. SKIPPIT is a platform that harnesses the full power of STOP Codon Readthrough elements, from both characterising them to making them into a tool: a first-in-class readthrough riboswitch.  STOP Codon Readthrough elements interact with the ribosome at the STOP codon site, leading to the STOP codon being decoded by a tRNA instead of the termination complex, allowing translation to continue beyond the STOP.  Designing this switch has only been possible thanks to the development of a cutting edge Software: TADPOLE. This software uses computationally-predicted RNA structures to optimise the design of RNA switches from just two RNA sequences.

title: KIT: CRC-Killer In and ouT
text: KIT: CRC-Killer In and ouT. Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most common cancer and the second leading cause of cancer death globally. Despite advances in chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, treatment remains limited by drug resistance and toxicity. This study presents the “CRC-killer in and out” integrated delivery kit, combining endogenous oral capsules with engineered bacteria and exogenous intelligent microneedle patches for comprehensive CRC therapy. The “in” module enhances intestinal targeting and bioavailability via peptide-mediated accumulation, while the “out” module employs minimally invasive microneedles with iontophoresis-enhanced transdermal delivery and responsive drug release. Together, they enable individualized administration, improved compliance, and non-professional usability. The dual-path system merges home-use convenience with scalable applicability, reducing medical burdens， which offer an innovative approach for CRC home-based and large-scale treatment.

title: CO2llectors—Overexpressing cmpABCD Fusion Bicarbonate Transporters Improves the Carbon Concentrating Mechanism in Cyanobacteria
text: CO2llectors—Overexpressing cmpABCD Fusion Bicarbonate Transporters Improves the Carbon Concentrating Mechanism in Cyanobacteria. Greenhouse gas emission is a major factor driving climate change. Considering the limitations of conventional mitigation approaches, our team proposed a synthetic biology approach by genetically modifying cyanobacteria Synechococcus elongatus PCC 7942 to enhance CO2 fixation efficiency. Our strategy involves overexpressing the cmpAB and CD fusion genes containing a light-sensitive promoter to increase the amount of bicarbonate transporter 1 (BCT1) within the cyanobacterial carbon concentrating mechanism (CCM). Ultimately, we aim to increase inorganic carbon uptake and saturate RuBisCO’s CO2 binding sites, facilitating photosynthetic CO2 sequestration. Coupling protein modeling and functional assays performed on wild-type cyanobacteria to obtain a dry lab model quantifying the cyanobacterial carbon intake, we envision integrating the engineered cyanobacteria into a carbon fixation photobioreactor. In addition, besides evaluating the scalability and sustainability of our hardware from a scientific and economic perspective, we also extended our outreach into the local and global community by educating about synthetic biology.

title: Pestacheck: An Improved Pesticide Residue Detection Test Strip
text: Pestacheck: An Improved Pesticide Residue Detection Test Strip. Pesticide residues on food pose serious health risks to the whole world, yet current detection methods remain inefficient and unstable. Recognizing this issue, we developed Pestacheck, a rapid, low-cost pesticide residue detection test strip based on the enzyme-inhibition principle of acetylcholinesterase (AChE). Through Alanine-scanning mutagenesis, we engineered AChE mutants via Cell-Free expression system. The optimized enzyme was immobilized with Gold Nanoparticles (AuNP) to improve sensitivity and integrated into a colloidal gold-based test strip for visible colorimetric detection. Together, Pestacheck provides a user-friendly synthetic biology solution for on-site pesticide residue detection.

title: LarVase: Bioengineering Cellulase with YebF-Mediated Secretion for Sustainable Manufacturing and Efficient Food Waste Degradation
text: LarVase: Bioengineering Cellulase with YebF-Mediated Secretion for Sustainable Manufacturing and Efficient Food Waste Degradation. Food waste has a huge impact on our planet. It destroys habitats, emits huge amounts of greenhouse gases, and threatens society deeply. Currently, one of the most sustainable methods is using black soldier fly larvae to degrade food waste. However, black soldier fly larvae are unable to efficiently digest cellulose, suggesting that improving the degradation process could enhance overall conversion efficiency and lower the costs associated with food waste treatment. LarVase aims to mass-produce endo-1,4-β-glucanase, a cellulase originating from Bacillus subtilis, through cloning into an E. coli BL21 expression vector. With our specially designed plasmids, we used YebF, a carrier protein having a similar function as a signal peptide, to be able to transport endo-1,4-β-glucanase outside the cell. This will lower the current costs of enzyme production while maintaining environmental sustainability.

title: PestiGuard - The Smart Aptamer Biosensor
text: PestiGuard - The Smart Aptamer Biosensor. PestiGuard is an innovative biosensor that puts food safety directly into the hands of consumers. To address the global health risks from pesticide residues, we have developed a simple, on-site detection system. At its heart are engineered bacteria containing a specialized RNA aptamer. When a specific pesticide is present, it binds to the aptamer, suppressing a fluorescent reporter gene and resulting in a dimmer glow. This provides an intuitive visual signal: brighter means safer, dimmer means contaminated. For precise results, we created companion software and hardware. A photo of the test sample is instantly analyzed, comparing the color intensity to a safety reference to display clear contamination levels. By integrating synthetic biology with smart technology, PestiGuard transforms complex lab testing into an accessible, user-friendly process, empowering everyone to make informed decisions about their food.

title: SPROUT - Smart Peptide Release On Unique Triggers
text: SPROUT - Smart Peptide Release On Unique Triggers. Fungal pathogens pose a major threat to agriculture, causing significant economic losses and straining global food systems. Climate change worsens these challenges by creating warmer, more humid conditions that favor fungal infections. Conventional fungicides often harm beneficial organisms, disrupt ecosystems, and drive pathogen resistance, threatening long-term food security. We propose a more precise and sustainable alternative. Using a modular sensor system with a genetic AND-gate, our engineered bacteria detect pathogen-specific signals tied to physiology and secretome, releasing antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) only when needed. This ensures targeted action while minimizing off-target effects. SPROUT is a scalable, precision-based platform for next-generation plant protection. Its modular design allows easy adaptation to diverse crops and pathogens, enabling efficient, on-demand AMP release. By combining specificity, adaptability, and sustainability, SPROUT offers a practical and innovative approach to strengthening agricultural resilience against fungal diseases.

title: Xylego
text: Xylego. We developed Xylego, an engineered E. coli Nissle 1917 designed as a low-burden synbiotic therapy for Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD). Xylego integrates three key modules: (1) Colonization support – enables selective growth using xylitol, reducing administration frequency; (2) Mucosal healing – secretes epidermal growth factor (EGF) to promote epithelial repair and break the inflammatory cycle; and (3) Inflammation-dependent kill switch – a tetrathionate-sensing restriction–modification system that self-destructs after inflammation resolves, preventing long-term risks and antibiotic gene transfer. Xylego is expected to enhance remission rates, improve adherence, and provide a safe, adaptable platform for patient-tailored probiotic therapies.

title: AureoLyze
text: AureoLyze. Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) forms biofilms that protect bacterial cells and confer strong resistance to antibiotics, making them a major cause of chronic and persistent infections. These infections are particularly harmful in immunocompromised patients, exacerbating conditions such as cystic fibrosis, tuberculosis, and catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs). Staphylococcus epidermidis (S. epidermidis), a common skin commensal, secretes an extracellular serine protease (Esp) capable of cleaving autolysin, an essential factor in biofilm formation responsible for extracellular DNA (eDNA) release, which enhances biofilm stability. However, Esp also targets human biofilm components and other host proteins, limiting its therapeutic potential. To make Esp a viable therapeutic agent, it must selectively cleave bacterial biofilm proteins—specifically, autolysin—without degrading human substrates. To achieve this, we aim to engineer Esp through site-directed mutagenesis (SDM) to enhance its substrate specificity toward the autolysin. By introducing targeted mutations based on Esp–autolysin (Atl) interaction analyses, we seek to reduce its off-target activity against human proteins while maintaining its biofilm-degrading capability, enabling its safe use as an anti-biofilm therapeutic.

title: ClaresO: Purification of Martian water from toxic perchlorate.
text: ClaresO: Purification of Martian water from toxic perchlorate.. Mars has long fascinated humankind. With the growing interest in its exploration, the use of local resources, especially water, is becoming increasingly important. However, its huge natural water resources are contaminated by toxic perchlorate salts and thus unusable.  Therefore, we engineer Bacillus subtilis 168 to detoxify perchlorate fully and convert it into harmless chloride and oxygen. To measure perchlorate concentrations, we established an in vivo perchlorate quantification assay that functions via organic phase extraction.  To understand the underlying biochemistry, we characterized perchlorate degradation enzymes in vitro and investigated the effect of rational mutations to improve their performance.  To enable practical implementation of our project, we built and tested a low-cost DIY anaerobic bioreactor. In order to simulate Martian microgravity, we designed, built and verified a random positioning machine from scratch. This device enables biological studies in simulated microgravity environments.

title: Nereis
text: Nereis. Nereis' project focuses on conserving the marine environment by degrading the pollutant naphthalene, a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). We identified salt-tolerant genes encoding proteins that help organisms survive in high sodium environments, as well as a catabolic pathway that uses naphthalene as a carbon source. Our goal is to genetically modify Pseudomonas putida, to be both salt-tolerant and capable of enhanced naphthalene degradation. These modification would allow the bacteria to function effectively in marine conditions. The naphthalene degradation pathway is found in P.putida G7, specifically in the NAH7 plasmid, which encodes the necessary degrading enzymes. Major challenges include adapting P. putida to high sodium concentration and introducing the large NAH7 plasmid. First, we will modified the bacteria with salt tolerant genes and test its tolerance to different sodium concentration. Second, we want to introduce the degrading enzymes in the salt-tolerant strain and assess the effectiveness of naphthalene degradation.

title: TroGen: A commensal bacterial platform for intracellular drug delivery in TNBC
text: TroGen: A commensal bacterial platform for intracellular drug delivery in TNBC. Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is the most aggressive subtype, with rapid progression, poor prognosis, and no effective targeted therapies, highlighting urgent need for new strategies.  Building on Prof. Shang Cai’s work on intracellular commensal bacteria—especially the tumor-targeting potential of Staphylococcus—we developed TroGen, an intracellular delivery platform using engineered commensals. To enhance invasion, we introduced the `fnbA` gene into non-pathogenic Staphylococcus to express S. aureus FnBPA, exploiting integrin-mediated endocytosis for efficient TNBC entry. Two biosafety modules confine bacterial survival and therapeutic payload expression to the tumor microenvironment.  Using AlphaFold-Multimer, MD, MM/PBSA, and phylogenetic analysis, we selected the optimal FnBP from multiple candidates. We formulated a reaction–diffusion–convection coupled PDE and used COMSOL Multiphysics to simulate intratumoral bacterial diffusion.  Human Practices informed iterative design, and outreach activities fostered scientific curiosity.

title: Antitumor Immunotherapy Using Guanylate Cyclase-Based Engineered Bacteria to Target the STING Pathway in Macrophages
text: Antitumor Immunotherapy Using Guanylate Cyclase-Based Engineered Bacteria to Target the STING Pathway in Macrophages. Colorectal cancer (CRC) is characterized by an immunosuppressive, hypoxic tumor microenvironment (TME) dominated by M2 macrophages. To address this, we engineered the probiotic E. coli Nissle 1917 (EcN) as a targeted living therapeutic. Our engineered auxotrophic EcN strain incorporates two synthetic genetic circuits: a hypoxia-responsive plasmid for tumor-specific production of the STING agonist c-di-GMP, and a synthetic "suicide" circuit for AHL-inducible bacterial lysis and payload release with essential metabolic gene thyA and dapA knockout. This triple system ensures precise immune activation within the tumor and provides a crucial biocontainment mechanism. We further developed a mathematical model to simulate AHL diffusion and its kinetic relationship with therapy, and designed a gut-on-a-chip device for physiologically relevant testing. This work establishes a safe, modular platform for targeted CRC immunotherapy.

title: ARMOR: Astro-Resilient Multi-Operational Recombinant-gel
text: ARMOR: Astro-Resilient Multi-Operational Recombinant-gel. Space exploration requires lightweight and durable materials to be manufactured in situ. Current chemical-based materials rely heavily on Earth supply chains. To address this gap, we engineered fusion proteins combining hagfish intermediate filament (HIF) and mussel foot protein (MFP) domains. Expression was induced in E. coli BL21 (DE3) and proteins were purified using Ni–NTA column. The best estimated yield reached 193 mg/ml. Co-assembly showed hydrogel formation, and the adhesive performance quantified by maximum force measurement recorded strength near 20,000 N/m², comparable to commercial glues. Adhesion was strong at space walking temperature (120 °C) but rapidly decline when below –20 °C. We developed SHIELD—a 3D-printed, low-cost fermentation device achieving cell densities upto OD600~20. Besides, we modified the fusion protein's structure, removing one of the terminal domains, and explored the structure-property relationships with preliminary results. With ARMOR, we are excited for the potential of syn-bio for next-generation space materials.

title: Project Opthera
text: Project Opthera. Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is a leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, characterized by progressive optic nerve damage and often asymptomatic until significant vision loss occurs. Current treatments primarily address elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) but fail to halt the underlying retinal ganglion cell (RGC) degeneration. To address this dual pathology, we developed a novel, non-invasive eye drop formulation containing two fusion peptides: FT, which lowers IOP, and BC, which provides neuroprotection by reducing RGC apoptosis. This dual-therapy approach simultaneously targets both key disease mechanisms, offering a more comprehensive strategy to slow glaucoma progression. Our project integrated human practices to ensure viability and societal impact. We engaged patients, clinicians, and bioethicists to refine our work ethically. Through stakeholder dialogue and targeted outreach, we balanced diverse needs and raised glaucoma awareness. This created a positive feedback loop, strengthening our project's purpose and laying the groundwork for future innovation.

title: NitroDuck
text: NitroDuck. Dairy farmers are struggling to keep their farms profitable - the protein feed, the most crucial element, is also one of the most expensive components for them. The most popular protein source is soybean. It contributed to the loss of natural ecosystems in Brazil's tropical savanna. Duckweed, the fastest-growing plant on Earth, contains as much protein as soybeans and grows 10x faster. It is set to provide an affordable protein source for every farm. But duckweed, as promising as it looks, cannot match 3000 years of selective breeding of soybeans. To make it a crop, we need SynBio. We are developing a method for 5x faster genetic engineering of duckweed, constructing an autonomous cultivation system and a yield prediction model, simplifying the scaling of duckweed. The first steps toward unlocking the massive potential of this tiny plant… To save farmers' money, the Cerrado savanna, and to make plants truly scalable.

title: DR. sTraTeGY: Engineering Multicellular Yeast for Drug Resistance Mutation Tracking
text: DR. sTraTeGY: Engineering Multicellular Yeast for Drug Resistance Mutation Tracking. DR. sTraTeGY is built on "Grape Yeast" chassis, designed to track fungal drug resistance mutations. It transforms the evolution of fungi from a static snapshot into an observable spatio-temporal lineage tree. Its current version has two functions: mutation event recording and cell lineage tracing. Our optimized transcription unit - pSTM1-driven EMSfp499, combines a mutation-sensitive promoter with an EMS-resistant fluorescent protein, enabling high-fidelity recording of mutation dynamics. We developed YeastVerse, a modeling and simulation tool, to predict key parameters such as fluorescent protein expression and maturation, which allows dry-lab simulation to guide subsequent wet-lab experiments. In addition, we have established a DBTL cycle that integrates mathematical modeling with AI-assisted reasoning.   We engage rare disease communities, through collaborative art and sensory-inclusive activities, fostering an accessible and participatory scientific environment. By integrating synthetic biology, computing, and community engagements, DR. sTraTeGY provides a new strategy to address the global challenge of fungal drug resistance.

title: Targeting DDRs: Modular Biomanufacturing of Collagen
text: Targeting DDRs: Modular Biomanufacturing of Collagen. Type III collagen (COLIII) not only supports tissue elasticity but also regulates the tumor microenvironment by transmitting dormancy signals to cancer cells. To overcome the limitations of animal-derived collagen, we established a synthetic-biology-based microbial production system to produce humanized COLIII, achieving biosafety and functional customization. By introducing the GVMGFO motif, a specific binding site for Discoidin Domain Receptor 1 (DDR1), we engineered COLIII to precisely target DDR1 on tumor cell surfaces. Using molecular modeling, docking, and dynamics simulations, we selected the recombinant COLIII variant (rCOL III) with the most stable structure and highest binding affinity for DDR1.The selected rCOL III was successfully expressed in Pichia pastoris and showed preliminary intervention effects on breast cancer cells in vitro, demonstrating a potential inhibitory role. This project integrates synthetic biology, protein engineering, and computational design, providing a green and modular biomaterial strategy for breast cancer intervention and prevention.

title: PhytClub
text: PhytClub. Pepper foot rot is a devastating disease that affects black pepper (P. nigrum) vines. Caused by the oomycete Phytophthora capsici, the infection leads to extensive yield loss and mortality in Karnataka and Kerala. Globally, plantations in Vietnam and Indonesia also suffer a similar fate. Chemical fungicides and current biocontrol measures are ineffective and unsustainable, driving the need for an innovative solution.  MIT-MAHE has developed a targeted, preventative solution that curbs foot rot. PhytClub implements small interfering RNA (siRNA) that are specifically designed to silence the bZIP transcription factor in P. capsici, through the RNA interference mechanism. Chitosan nanoparticles encapsulate the siRNA to confer stability and aid their uptake into the pathogen. Furthermore, the team has automated the siRNA design process and combined it with a model that predicts the stability of an siRNA-nanoparticle complex, providing a foundational software tool that helps future researchers seamlessly build gene silencing systems.

title: LOGIC: Lasting Optimized Genetic Input Calculator
text: LOGIC: Lasting Optimized Genetic Input Calculator. Biological computing holds great promise, yet past engineered bacterial circuits for logic gates have suffered from excessive complexity, cumbersome operation, and reliance on multiple input substances. Our LOGIC project overcomes these problems by developing a novel approach to constructing a biocomputer—utilizing quorum sensing and spatial diffusion to form logic gates. For addition calculation, we construct high-pass and band-pass genetic circuits based on the quorum sensing (QS) system. Through the diffusion of QS molecules in solid media, we can build various logic gates and connect them to perform multi-bit binary calculations. For repetitive operation, we engineer a light-induced QS molecule degradation enzyme and a protein degradation tag to refresh the calculator. Building upon the calculator, we can also build accessories like result storage, decimal result display and latches, demonstrating its extensive prospects. Furthermore, we construct a LOGIC Toolkit with visualization software for future research.

title: PROTATO: Proteolysis-based Detection for Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato Affected Tomato
text: PROTATO: Proteolysis-based Detection for Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato Affected Tomato. Early detection of plant pathogens is essential for reducing crop losses, yet most diagnostic systems remain laboratory-bound. We developed PROTATO: Proteolysis-based Detection for Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato Affected Tomato, a cell-free and protein logic–based biosensing platform enabling on-site pathogen detection. PROTATO integrates a coiled-coil–mediated chain exchange reaction as its molecular logic core and a dual-input AND gate that responds specifically to the pathogen effector AvrRpt2 protease and the phytotoxin coronatine (COR), reconstituting split luciferase, GFP, or trehalase reporters. A positive-feedback loop amplifies protease activity, improving detection sensitivity and signal strength. To enable field deployment, we engineered the PROTATO KIT, a 3D-printed electrochemical device that converts glucose signals into electronic readouts via glucose oxidase–modified electrodes and microcontrollers. Portable (Air) and scalable (Pro) versions support diverse agricultural applications. Our project establishes a generalizable framework for cell-free protein logic, advancing low-cost biosensing for crop protection and beyond.

title: Com-bat-ing White-Nose Syndrome: Engineering E. coli to Secrete Protease Inhibitors Against Pseudogymnoascus destructans
text: Com-bat-ing White-Nose Syndrome: Engineering E. coli to Secrete Protease Inhibitors Against Pseudogymnoascus destructans. Pseudogymnoascus destructans is a pathogenic fungus that causes White-nose syndrome (WNS), one of the most devastating wildlife diseases in modern history, responsible for mass bat mortality across North America. Locally in Michigan, 5 of our 9 bat species are affected--with repercussions for biodiversity, agriculture, public health, and environmental stability. WNS develops in bats during their hibernation period when proteolytic enzymes produced by the fungus degrade the collagen in their nose, ears, and wings, causing them to wake prematurely from wintertime hibernation, leading to energy depletion, lethargy, and death by starvation due to the lack of necessary resources in winter. There are no effective treatments currently. We propose engineering Escherichia coli to secrete serine protease inhibitor(s) targeting the virulence factor of the fungus. These inhibitors would block collagen degradation, allowing bats to maintain uninterrupted hibernation, thus improving survival outcomes for one of our most essential, if silent allies.

title: Snaccine
text: Snaccine. Snaccine is a novel type of vaccine, ideal for vaccinating chickens against avian influenza (bird flu). Genetically modified bacteriophages are taken orally, in a stomach acid-resistant pill. They reproduce inside gut bacteria, while also producing RNA packaged within armour (an MS2 virus-like particle coated with cell-penetrating peptides). This RNA enters (eukaryotic) host cells and works just like an mRNA vaccine, tricking the cell into producing an antigen. This antigen is detected by the immune system and teaches it to recognise and fight the original pathogen. Snaccines share many of the same advantages that mRNA technology has over traditional vaccines. But where typical mRNA vaccines have to be kept in freezers, Snaccines can be stored and transported at room temperature. Together with their cheaper production and oral administration route, Snaccine is an ideal technology for fighting bird flu.

title: BEATS：a Biohybrid Engineered Anti-cancer Therapeutic Serratia
text: BEATS：a Biohybrid Engineered Anti-cancer Therapeutic Serratia. This project addresses the critical challenges of drug resistance and systemic toxicity in conventional cancer therapy by developing a novel live bacterial delivery system based on an engineered Serratia marcescens strain. We leveraged the native capacity of this bacterium to synthesize prodigiosin—a potent antitumor compound—while implementing biosafety enhancements through msbB gene knockout to reduce endotoxin production. For precise tumor targeting, we functionalized the attenuated strain with carboxymethyl cellulose encapsulation and the KP101 homing peptide. To support quantitative analysis and predictive modeling, we developed a comprehensive computational toolkit including an automated fluorescence image segmentation pipeline, a ConvLSTM-based spatiotemporal prediction model, and the integrated OncoPredict Suite platform. Guided by responsible innovation and the SEEK framework, our project combines synthetic biology with translational tool development to offer a targeted and adaptable strategy for next-generation cancer treatment

title: Trashformers - Enzymatic Glycolysis of Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) textile fibres, and upcycling of terephthalic acid.
text: Trashformers - Enzymatic Glycolysis of Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) textile fibres, and upcycling of terephthalic acid.. Polyethylene terephthalate (PET), the main component of polyester textiles, dominates global fiber production and generates millions of tons of waste annually. Current recycling methods rely on energy-intensive chemical processes. Our project, Trashformers, tackles this challenge by developing a synthetic biology system for PET textile recycling and upcycling, designed to provide all the reaction components needed for efficient depolymerization and upcycling. We focus on enzymatic glycolysis to depolymerize PET into bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (BHET), a monomer suited for re-polymerization. To achieve this, we designed a system based on E. coli BL21(DE3) and devices utilizing PETase hydrolases. We design two complementary systems in parallel. The first employs enzymatic hydrolysis to degrade PET into terephthalic acid (TPA), and ethylene glycol required for subsequent glycolysis. The second uses rational enzyme design to create a novel enzyme that activates TPA with coenzyme A  Paving the way for PET upcycling through metabolic and chemical valorization.

title: DopaMine: Engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae for Self-Regulated L-DOPA Biosynthesis: A SynBio Approach to Parkinson's Disease Treatment
text: DopaMine: Engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae for Self-Regulated L-DOPA Biosynthesis: A SynBio Approach to Parkinson's Disease Treatment. Parkinson’s Disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons, leading to motor impairments such as tremors and rigidity. Current treatments rely on L-DOPA supplementation, but long-term use results in decreased efficacy and severe side effects. To address these limitations, we propose engineering Saccharomyces cerevisiae (S. cerevisiae) to biosynthesize and regulate L-DOPA production using the yeast codon-optimized CYP76AD6 gene from Beta vulgaris partnered with the AR2 gene from Arabidopsis thaliana. By integrating metabolic engineering and synthetic biology, our system aims to improve L-DOPA bioavailability while reducing treatment-related complications. The system incorporates sophisticated feedback mechanisms to maintain optimal L-DOPA levels, offering a potentially groundbreaking approach to PD therapy.

title: Totally [Fe]rocious
text: Totally [Fe]rocious. Antimicrobial resistance is currently a major global health crisis. To counter this issue, alternatives to antibiotics must be developed. One promising strategy involves the use of siderophores, iron-chelating molecules naturally synthesized by bacteria. We aimed to hack this system by adding a gold nanoparticle to one of Klebsiella pneumoniae’s siderophores, aerobactin. These nanoparticles can then be activated with NIR lasers to kill bacteria. Our team focused on cloning aerobactin in Escherichia coli. We also performed in silico analyses to optimize aerobactin biosynthesis and deepen our understanding of the siderophore’s internalization by K. pneumoniae. A genome-scale metabolic analysis of aerobactin’s citrate production, along with biomolecular modeling of the TonB-dependent transporter embedded in the gram-negative bacterial membrane, was conducted. The next steps of this project would involve the synthesis of gold nanoparticles followed by their conjugation with aerobactin.

title: AromaWell: Customize Your Signature Aromatherapy Essential Oil
text: AromaWell: Customize Your Signature Aromatherapy Essential Oil. The core components of rose essential oil are geraniol and citronellol, while that of lavender is linalool. These three components share highly similar terpenoid biosynthetic pathways. This commonality provides us with an unprecedented technical opportunity: by modifying microbial cell factories, we enable yeast to produce geraniol (the common precursor substance) and Escherichia coli to synthesize citronellol and linalool. By enhancing the supply of precursor substances and introducing selective catalytic enzymes, we construct a metabolic network that can efficiently synthesize geraniol, citronellol, and linalool. The key lies in the introduction of regulatable promoter systems and artificial gene circuits, which allow for precise regulation of the metabolic flux of each synthetic branch through external induction and culture parameters. This enables end-users to dynamically adjust the synthesis rate of each component according to their personal preferences, and ultimately obtain personalized mixed essential oil components in a single fermentation system at one time.

title: E.P.I.C : Epigenetic Programmable Intervention & Control
text: E.P.I.C : Epigenetic Programmable Intervention & Control. Targeted DNA methylation is a promising approach for programmable gene regulation. To explore this, we designed and expressed a novel fusion protein, dCas9-Dam (DNA adenine methyltransferase), in E. coli. dCas9 was directed to user-specified loci with the help of guide RNA, enabling targeted adenine methylation at GATC sites. We constructed a plasmid encoding dCas9-Dam with guide RNA and a reporter plasmid containing a GFP gene downstream of a methylation-sensitive promoter. Co-transfection into E. coli allowed us to assess whether dCas9-Dam could induce targeted methylation and regulate GFP expression. Our results will test the ability of dCas9-Dam to perform locus-specific DNA methylation and alter reporter gene expression.The system can be extended to other methyltransferases in bacteria, opening avenues for applications in biomanufacturing, therapeutics, and diagnostics. By enabling precise epigenetic editing, this approach holds potential for developing novel treatments for diseases linked to aberrant methylation, such as cancer, neurodegenerative disorders,and imprinting-related syndromes

title: Optimizing Heparosan Biosynthesis in E. coli BL21 By Use of an RBS Library
text: Optimizing Heparosan Biosynthesis in E. coli BL21 By Use of an RBS Library. Heparosan is a key polysaccharide precursor in the synthesis of heparin, an essential anticoagulant widely used in medicine. However, current methods of heparosan production rely on inefficient microbial strains. Our project aims to design and optimize synthesis of heparosan in a more commonly used strain - BL21 (DE3). We are reconstructing the heparosan synthesis pathway found in E. coli K5 by expressing four essential genes—kfiA, kfiB, kfiC, and kfiD, and inserting them onto a single plasmid, incorporating a library of degenerate ribosome binding sites (RBS) on our primers. Using degenerate DNA sequences for our RBS allows us to synthesize a library of varying ribosomal binding affinity for each gene, which in turn, gives us a wide range of gene expression. This allows us to determine the optimal activity level for each gene to produce the most heparosan.

title: ILXIR: IL-10 In Response
text: ILXIR: IL-10 In Response. Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) is a chronic condition characterized by inflammation in the gastrointestinal tract. The cause of IBD is an overreactive immune response, leading to prolonged inflammation and tissue damage. A key regulator of such inflammation, Interleukin-10 (IL-10), plays a fundamental role in modulating inflammation and maintaining cell homeostasis by protecting the body from an uncontrolled immune response by inhibiting pro-inflammatory cytokines like TNF-α and IL-6. However, IL-10’s therapeutic potential is severely limited by its structural instability due to its homodimer nature and easy degradation within the body. This instability reduces its effectiveness as a long-term treatment leaving patients with limited options for prolonged IBD treatments. To address this issue, we propose a probiotic-based approach, engineering a mutated more stable form of Il-10 (MIL-10). Delivered through dairy products like yogurt, this system would provide MIL-10 production in reaction to pro-inflammatory cytokines, ensuring sustained inflammation control for diseases like IBD.

title: ExAway: A Protein Binding Inhibitor for Exotoxin A
text: ExAway: A Protein Binding Inhibitor for Exotoxin A. Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) is a pathogenic bacterium that is responsible for an estimated 7% of all healthcare-associated infections. Exotoxin A (ETA) is one major virulence factor of PA. As a result, therapeutics targeting the inhibition of ETA activity are under development. ETA enters human cells through the CD91 receptor, activates via furin cleavage, and modifies eukaryotic elongation factor 2, inhibiting protein synthesis and inducing apoptosis. Although some inhibitors show signs of success, they consist of either small-molecule inhibitors, which have significant off-target effects, or antibodies, which cannot be produced efficiently due to size and folding properties. To address these limitations, we utilize RF diffusion, Protein MPNN, and AlphaFold to create a protein inhibitor that binds specifically to ETA's receptor binding domain. We tested these computationally designed inhibitors by expressing and purifying them, assessing their binding affinity to ETA and evaluating their ability to prevent ETA-mediated cell death using cell-based assays.

title: Oncoligo: Modular Antisense Oligonucleotide Lung Cancer Treatment
text: Oncoligo: Modular Antisense Oligonucleotide Lung Cancer Treatment. Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide, and many patients still lack effective long-term treatment options. Oncoligo introduces a modular therapeutic platform that harnesses antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) to selectively silence essential cancer genes within a synthetic-lethality framework, enabling the targeting of tumor-suppressor-driven and intracellular cancers. Our computational pipeline integrates molecular dynamics, machine learning, and algorithmic optimization to design all parts of the platform. We specifically design potent ASOs, which are conjugated to antibodies for targeted delivery. Within each antibody, tumor-associated epitopes stimulate immune activation and memory. Experimentally, our designed ASOs outperform commercial ones, showing superior knockdown at the mRNA, protein, and cellular levels. In parallel, we optimized antibody expression systems and developed a dedicated software tool that facilitates ASO design across diverse genes and organisms. By uniting synthetic biology, computation, and entrepreneurship, Oncoligo pioneers a versatile, scalable framework for precision oncology - redefining how we treat cancer.

title: safeTEA: safe Targeted Extraction via Aptamers
text: safeTEA: safe Targeted Extraction via Aptamers. In order to address the global challenge of mycotoxin contamination in food and drink products, we aim to develop a detoxification system adaptable to diverse agricultural communities and food systems worldwide. Our methods focus on aflatoxin B1, the most carcinogenic mycotoxin and a major burden to resource-limited communities. Once bound, toxins can be removed through simple, inexpensive, and widely available cellulose-based materials that can be safely composted after use. As part of the plasmid design process, we introduce NOODL (Novel Optimization Of DNA Linkers), a Julia-based genetic algorithm that generates custom spacer sequences for single-stranded DNA. This tool simplifies spacer design by minimizing unwanted interactions and secondary structures between functional ssDNA components for synthetic biology applications. By combining computational design and genetic engineering, our work offers an impactful approach to improving food safety while providing adaptable tools that foster innovation across synthetic biology.

title: One Health Outaouais
text: One Health Outaouais. By 2050, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is expected to kill 10 million people each year, making it a major global threat. Here in Québec, our farmers follow strict rules for antibiotic use—they require a vet’s prescription. Even with these measures, resistant bacteria still emerge, particularly in manure and wastewater. When we started our One Health Outaouais (OHO) project, our plan was to develop a test for AMR genes to map the region’s resistome. But conversations with farmers, veterinarians, and experts helped us realize our approach was too academic. They didn’t need more data; they needed practical tools to make better, faster decisions for their animals. So, we transformed our test into a product: the VIGIL | FARM platform. VIGIL | FARM will provide farmers with on-site rapid diagnostics and reliable information, helping them use antibiotics more precisely and only when necessary — protecting both animal health and public safety.

title: The Cysteinator — a biological device to enhance biohydrogen production.
text: The Cysteinator — a biological device to enhance biohydrogen production.. The effects of climate change underscore the need to develop sustainable energy technology. Hydrogen (H2) based sustainable energy solutions decarbonize high-heat industrial processes and long-distance transport. However, current H2 production is land and water-intensive, and largely reliant on fossil fuels. Dark Fermentation (DF)—an anaerobic process where glucose is converted to H2—is a sustainable alternative that can be integrated into waste-to-energy (WTE) streams. Currently, DF cannot produce H2 in commercially viable quantities. Our device, “The Cysteinator”, solves this challenge by supplementing DF bioreactor feedstocks with precise concentrations of L-cysteine. L-cysteine lowers the oxidation-reduction potential in DF feedstocks, helping hydrogen-producing bacteria propagate and increasing hydrogenase function. Our device is accompanied by a multi-scale model that characterizes its behavior and informs its implementation in a variety of WTE streams. Our project includes thorough analyses on the Cysteinator’s impact on WTE streams, DF market viability, and the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals.

title: Microbial Electrosynthesis of Glycerol from CO₂ via Engineered Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans
text: Microbial Electrosynthesis of Glycerol from CO₂ via Engineered Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans. Facing the dual challenges of greenhouse gas accumulation and renewable energy intermittency, electrochemical CO₂ reduction presents a promising solution by converting electrical energy into storable chemicals. The CUG-China 2025 project engineers the acidophilic bacterium Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans – which naturally thrives in extreme acidic conditions (pH<2) – to create a novel electricity-driven carbon fixation platform. This engineered strain incorporates three key synthetic modules: enhanced extracellular electron uptake, efficient glycerol synthesis from fixed carbon, and optimized CO₂ fixation via the Calvin cycle. When integrated into a microbial electrochemical system, the platform achieves efficient CO₂ conversion while producing valuable chemicals, offering a sustainable approach to simultaneous carbon mitigation and energy storage.

title: NRPieceS - Unlocking Nature's Antibiotic Toolbox
text: NRPieceS - Unlocking Nature's Antibiotic Toolbox. We present NRPieceS, a versatile synthetic biology platform for rapid generation of large non-ribosomal peptide (NRP) libraries with minimal cloning effort. By integrating advanced NRPS engineering techniques, NRPieceS enables efficient combinatorial biosynthesis of potential bioactive peptides. The platform encompasses a complete Design-Build-Test-Learn workflow, including heterologous expression, derivatization, activity screening, and computational guidance through our software mATChmaker. The accompanying plasmid collection (160 plasmids, including 35 donor constructs) facilitates modular NRPS assembly and rational engineering. mATChmaker models and visualizes native and hybrid NRPS condensation complexes, providing structural and phylogenetic insights to guide module compatibility and design. Using NRPieceS, we generated and screened peptide libraries against ESKAPE pathogens, identifying antimicrobial hits. Furthermore, a Trojan horse strategy employing siderophore conjugation via click chemistry might enhance bacterial uptake. NRPieceS unites wet-lab and computational tools in a sustainable framework, accelerating antibiotic discovery and enabling accessible NRPS engineering for the broader research community.

title: PlasMission: Re-sensitizing Beta-Lactam Resistant Bacteria
text: PlasMission: Re-sensitizing Beta-Lactam Resistant Bacteria. Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a critical global threat, causing 1.27 million deaths annually and projected to reach 10 million per year by 2050. To address β-lactamase–mediated resistance, PlasMission engineered a conjugative microbial system that transfers a plasmid encoding Beta-Lactamase Inhibitory Protein (BLIP) between bacteria. BLIP binds to β-lactamase enzymes, restoring bacterial sensitivity to β-lactam antibiotics. Using E. coli S17-1 as the donor, our system successfully delivered BLIP-I and BLIP-II plasmids into E. coli DH5α, causing ampicillin-resistant recipients to lose viability under antibiotic selection. We envision expanding this system into a conditional survival circuit with inducible BLIP expression, enhancing biosafety and enabling applications in biocontainment, therapeutic bacteria, and biosensing. Ultimately, our S17-1_BLIP system serves as a promising synthetic biology tool for re-sensitizing resistant bacteria, supporting rapid resistance detection, and contributing to safer, programmable antimicrobial interventions.

title: DuCon：A Dual-microbe system for vinasse recycling through Conversion to succinate
text: DuCon：A Dual-microbe system for vinasse recycling through Conversion to succinate. The treatment of Baijiu vinasse, which contains hard-to-degrade carbon sources, is a significant environmental challenge. For our iGEM project, we designed an innovative dual-microbe system to tackle this issue and produce high-value succinate. We genetically engineered Trichoderma reesei to secrete laccase (from white rot fungus) and its native cellulase. This enables the simultaneous breakdown of lignin into short arenes and cellulose within the vinasse. Subsequently, the engineered Pseudomonas putida is introduced to uptake these arenes and direct them into its modified TCA cycle. We specifically engineered this pathway to overproduce succinate and added an efflux channel for its secretion. This system promises efficient vinasse decomposition while generating a valuable chemical, balancing environmental sustainability with economic benefit.

title: Revitalyze: Restoring Glycosylation, One Vesicle at a Time
text: Revitalyze: Restoring Glycosylation, One Vesicle at a Time. Congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDGs) are a group of rare metabolic diseases caused by defects in various stages of the glycosylation pathway. Errors in glycosylation can confuse cellular interactions, causing serious malfunctions in multiple organs and organ systems. The most common type of CDG is PMM2-CDG (or CDG-Ia), where the mutation in the PMM2 enzyme, which converts mannose-6-phosphate to mannose-1-phosphate, leads to decreased glycosylation rate. As a comprehensive solution to this problem, Revitalyze proposes engineering probiotics that deliver the functional PMM2 protein to the patient’s body cells via bacterial extracellular vesicles (bEVs), thereby allowing an enzyme replacement therapy that minimizes disruption in the patients' daily lives. Starting with PMM2-CDG, our delivery system can be expanded to any other type of CDG caused by mutations in enzymes, and potentially other disorders as well. Revitalyze is more than a treatment; it's a step toward hope for all rare disorders.

title: CONCAVE: Generating and Applying Antibody Alternatives
text: CONCAVE: Generating and Applying Antibody Alternatives. Antibodies play a crucial role in immunity by binding to specific antigens. Despite their widespread use, the production of antibodies remains costly and time-consuming, and dependent upon animal use. Our project, Concave, seeks to overcome these challenges by developing a modular synthetic biology platform to design customized binding proteins that mimic the versatility of antibodies and can be efficiently produced in E. coli. We are developing a scalable system for generating highly diverse leucine-rich repeat (LRR) proteins known as Repebodies, which are synthetic variants of lamprey VLRs that function similarly to antibodies. By combining this with retron-based mutagenesis, we enable continuous, in situ diversification of LRRs without manual intervention, allowing us to generate Repebodies that bind virtually any antigen.  In order to use the Repebodies’ target binding, we are designing Repebody-nanobody fusion proteins that interface with mammalian degradation machinery. This system is designed for degradation of membrane-bound or cytoplasmic proteins.

title: Pyricon - Spinning a Future with Spider Silk towards more sustainable construction materials
text: Pyricon - Spinning a Future with Spider Silk towards more sustainable construction materials. Cement production accounts for about 8% of global CO₂ emissions (Kajaste & Hurme, 2016), and demand is expected to rise (Castro-Alonso et al., 2019; Lanjewar et al., 2025). At Pyricon, we address this challenge by creating a sustainable, bio-based alternative to cement bricks. We engineer Bacillus subtilis to produce spider silk proteins that enhance microbially induced calcite precipitation by another bacterium, forming a durable biocement. Using a novel PCR-free DNA assembly strategy and codon harmonisation, we aim to efficiently express highly repetitive silk genes. Our approach not only enables eco-friendly construction materials but also advances synthetic biology by providing a robust method for assembling reptitive DNA sequences. Scaled adoption of Pyricon’s biocement could significantly cut embodied CO₂ in masonry and small-scale construction while extending material lifespan, offering a practical path toward a lower-carbon built environment.

title: STREAM
text: STREAM. Bioproduction forms the basis of industries from food to textiles and pharmaceuticals, yet fluctuations in metabolite output and limited access to advanced equipment remain major challenges. STREAM addresses these by integrating proof-of-concept metabolic control with affordable, modular hardware, open-access software, and a predictive model. Our system enhances continuous metabolite production through a ratiometric biosensor that monitors concentrations in real time, enabling feedback-driven control. When product formation declines, inducers are added to overcome pathway bottlenecks and stabilize productivity. A mathematical model simulates inducer effects and metabolic dynamics, while an optimization algorithm balances inducer use and yield to minimize costs.An intuitive open-source software allows for easy hardware control.  Together, these components demonstrate how low-cost, modular hardware combined with biosensor-guided feedback control can stabilize cultures, reduce metabolic stress, and enhance the reliability of bioproduction - making continuous bioprocessing more accessible, reproducible, and sustainable for teams and labs worldwide.

title: RhizoRetention: Creating drought-resistant Brassica napus through bacteria-mediated RNA interference
text: RhizoRetention: Creating drought-resistant Brassica napus through bacteria-mediated RNA interference. In Alberta, more than 14,000 farmers grow over 6.6 million acres of canola each year. As Canada’s most valuable crop, canola contributes nearly $30 billion annually to the economy. However, climate change, particularly persistent drought, threatens productivity. Developing drought-resistant canola could help secure the sector’s future. One promising strategy combines plant-growth-promoting rhizobacteria with RNA interference (RNAi) to silence genes that reduce drought tolerance. A 2020 study in Arabidopsis thaliana found that overexpression of the transcription factor bHLH61 impaired drought tolerance, while loss of function improved it. Since a homologous gene exists in canola, targeting it may enhance drought resistance. Our approach engineers Arthrobacter globiformis to produce small-interfering RNA (siRNA) against bHLH61. Incorporated into seed coatings, the bacteria colonize canola roots and deliver double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) to silence the gene. This method could improve drought resilience in canola and help mitigate the impacts of climate change.

title: ParkinSolve
text: ParkinSolve. Parkinson’s Disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by dopaminergic neuron loss and microglial-driven inflammation. Current treatments only alleviate symptoms without halting disease progression. To address this, we engineered CHO cells to secrete anti-inflammatory proteins (IL-1RA, IFNγR-Fc, and TLR4-Fc) that modulate microglial activation and protect neurons. Using a Tet-On 3G system, we achieved precise, doxycycline-inducible control of therapeutic protein expression. Conditioned media from transfected CHO cells improved BV2 microglial survival under rotenone-induced oxidative stress, with TLR4-Fc showing the strongest neuroprotective effect. This system demonstrates a controllable mammalian cell-based platform for adaptive, anti-inflammatory therapeutics in neurodegenerative disease.

title: UNIglobin: A Portable Enzymatic Kit for Universal Blood Conversion
text: UNIglobin: A Portable Enzymatic Kit for Universal Blood Conversion. As an essential medicine, blood should be “available at all times, in adequate amounts and in appropriate dosage forms, with assured quality and affordability,” according to the World Health Organization (WHO). However as it stands in 2024, blood still fails to meet the availability and safety qualities in over half the world’s countries. Our solution is a compact, field ready ABO blood conversion kit. We have identified, cloned, and characterized activity for glycoside hydrolase enzymes from Akkermansia muciniphila. These enzymes have the ability to cleave off the A and B blood antigens and their extended antigen groups and can be lyophilized for long term storage. Our complete kit also includes a filtering system made of biological materials to remove immune reactive white blood cells and a Miniaturized Electronic Antigen Biosensor (MEAB) for rapid quantification of ABO antigens. Together these technologies can process safe, universally compatible blood available, anytime, anywhere.

title: CERES: Computational Enzymes Research and Exploring System
text: CERES: Computational Enzymes Research and Exploring System. We developed a novel machine learning model named “LEAPS” that enables efficient protein function improvement from limited datasets. Conventional protein engineering requires large-scale experimental data, extensive expertise, and prolonged trial-and-error processes, making research execution heavily dependent on institutional funding and human resources. Consequently, significant barriers remain for student teams and small-scale laboratories attempting to engage in protein engineering. LEAPS substantially reduces these constraints and provides an accessible environment for researchers to perform multi-objective optimization of proteins. This model enables student teams participating in iGEM and researchers with limited resources to undertake functional improvements such as enzymatic activity enhancement and antibody affinity optimization, dramatically expanding research possibilities. Furthermore, we have developed and publicly released LEAPS as a web application, establishing a platform accessible to the broader research community. This model has the potential to promote data-driven protein engineering and accelerate research and development across all fields of life sciences.

title: Solving Barnacle adhesion to a ships hull through Biotechnology whilst expanding biotechnology learning.
text: Solving Barnacle adhesion to a ships hull through Biotechnology whilst expanding biotechnology learning.. We aimed to combat marine biofouling to reduce wasted fuel in the shipping industry caused by drag. We identified cp19k from previous iGEM projects as a key adhesive protein in barnacle cement. We optimised expression of cp19k in E. coli BL21 (DE3), then tested a range of proteases to identify which one(s) degrade it most effectively. This high school project did not benefit from usual university collaborations, and we attempted to complete all experiments in house, we created a programme to develop skills in younger students that would equip them for later involvement in the iGEM. We aimed for a safe, inclusive and collaborative environment advertising the team widely and keeping costs to a minimum for all. We have educated the school community and beyond through the iGEM process.

title: SAUR-eus
text: SAUR-eus. Antibiotic resistance is one of the biggest threats to modern medicine, and Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) stands at the center of this crisis. Conventional drugs are losing effectiveness, and broad-spectrum treatments often harm the beneficial bacteria we rely on. Our project takes a new angle: instead of fighting MRSA with traditional antibiotics, we use bioinformatics and computational modeling to uncover weak points in its biology using Staphylococcus aureus as a model organism. By mapping its genome and key metabolic pathways, we identify genes essential for building and maintaining its cell wall, which are targets that are unique to the pathogen and absent in healthy microbiota. With these insights, we aim to design next-generation antimicrobials that are precise, sustainable, and less likely to drive resistance. Project SAUR-eus isn’t just about tackling one superbug; it’s about rethinking how we fight infections while protecting the delicate balance of our microbial world.

title: AMADRYADS:A (CRISPR-Cas13d) Mediated Antifungal treatment ,Deploying a Riboswitch, Yielding Apoptotic Defense in a Systemic way.
text: AMADRYADS:A (CRISPR-Cas13d) Mediated Antifungal treatment ,Deploying a Riboswitch, Yielding Apoptotic Defense in a Systemic way.. Canker stain represents one of the most devastating threats to forest ecosystems worldwide, affecting all species of the genus Platanus, regardless of their size or age. It is a fungal disease caused by Ceratocystis platani. AMADRYADS is a chitosan-based nanocarrier system that encapsulates a plasmid. The plasmid cassette, delicately designed, contains a toehold-controlled Cas13d gene (a CRISPR/Cas ortholog that targets single-stranded RNA) and a gRNA array targeting two key fungal transcript, the products of the LysM and Res1 genes. With an emphasis on safety, we developed a non-GMO, biodegradable solution that operates on two specificity levels. First, it targets unique sequences found only in the fungus through gRNA modeling. Second, the toehold-controlled Cas13d gene is translated only in the presence of a species-specific toxin, ceratoplatanin (CP). Through these design features, combined with the high collateral activity characteristic of Cas13d, AMADRYADS aims to induce a total transcriptomic collapse of the pathogen.

title: Bioreactive heritage protection using engineered E.coli with enhanced sulfur reduction and biosilica coating
text: Bioreactive heritage protection using engineered E.coli with enhanced sulfur reduction and biosilica coating. Recently, more and more cultural heritage sites used microorganisms for biocleaning and protection. Our project leverages synthetic biology to develop a sustainable solution to protect heritage sites from environmental deterioration. Our project comprises two parts. Firstly, we addressed acid erosion by engineering sulphur reduction pathways. We engineered E. coli to reduce sulfate and sulfite to cysteine. We utilised two genes, YdeD, which exports cysteine out of bacterial cells, and YhaM, which degrades cysteine, to drive the reduction pathway. Secondly, we employed silicatein-expressed E. coli to catalyse the formation of biosilica from tetraethyl orthosilicate. This biosilica could fill cracks in structures and improve structural integrity. We also adopted csgA adhesion domain, which ensures our engineered E. coli adheres to building surfaces under acidic conditions. Together with our hardware for crack-repairing and models to estimate corrosion, we believe our project can bring new insights for future heritage protection projects utilising synthetic biology.

title: TRACE – Redefining STI testing through portable, paper-based diagnostics
text: TRACE – Redefining STI testing through portable, paper-based diagnostics. Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) remain a growing global health challenge. Despite being treatable when detected early, testing rates are low due to asymptomatic cases, limited awareness, high costs, and inconvenient diagnostics. TRACE reimagines STI testing through synthetic biology by developing a cell-free, paper-based self-test that works without laboratories or trained personnel, enabling frequent use in low-resource settings. By uniting accessibility, sensitivity, and ease of use, TRACE empowers individuals to test frequently, reduce transmission, and improve global sexual health. The system combines rapid, room-temperature nucleic acid amplification via recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with a specific colorimetric readout. Both CRISPR-Cas and a novel DNA hybridization-based detection approach were evaluated to optimize cost, durability, and specificity. Extensive human practices research guided design and implementation, incorporating feedback from users, healthcare providers, and stakeholders. Through modeling, stakeholder consultation, and market analysis, we ensure real-world feasibility.

title: Aquarius: Channeling SynBio from the Lab to Aquatic Environments
text: Aquarius: Channeling SynBio from the Lab to Aquatic Environments. The flow of water is essential to life on Earth, but can also carry negative consequences. Water movement transports pollutants to lakes, spreads harmful microbes through household plumbing, and corrodes infrastructure. Synthetic biology offers powerful solutions, yet few have been implemented in real-world aquatic environments. The lack of SynBio deployment in water environments stems from limited understanding of how engineered organisms function in dynamic environments, in which they must compete within native microbial communities, withstand shifting nutrient levels, and endure various physical stressors. Our project addresses this challenge through an integrated approach of chassis analysis software, predictive mathematical modeling, comprehensive RNA-seq meta-analysis and experimentation with engineered constructs in laboratory and aquatic settings. By analyzing how synthetic circuits behave in flowing water compared to laboratory settings, we uncover foundational design principles that will enable the development of safe, effective synthetic biology applications to tackle pressing global challenges linked to aquatic environments.

title: Sterosaurus
text: Sterosaurus. Our project proposes a novel system that tackles the climate crisis by repurposing carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions from manufacturing industries, transforming this waste into a valuable resource. Specifically, we utilize CO₂ to fuel algae bioreactors that produce high-value pharmaceutical compounds. By recycling industrial CO₂ and converting it into ergosterols, a precursor of steroid hormones, we create a circular economy model that emphasizes sustainability, innovation, and improved efficiency in pharmaceutical production.

title: CRIKIT: Developing a rapid CRISPR-based diagnostic kit for detecting antibiotic resistance
text: CRIKIT: Developing a rapid CRISPR-based diagnostic kit for detecting antibiotic resistance. Antibiotic resistance is one of the most critical emerging threats to global healthcare, with current projections indicating it will surpass cancer as a leading cause of mortality in the coming decades. Conventional methods for identifying antibiotic resistant infections are time-consuming, as they depend on culturing bacteria in the presence of antibiotics. This diagnosis delay often leads to trial-and-error treatment strategies, which not only compromise patient outcomes but also promote the spread of resistance. To address this challenge, we are developing CRIKIT, a rapid and versatile diagnostic tool based on using Cas13 and programmable guide RNAs (gRNAs) directly from cell lysate to target bacterial transcripts of specific antibiotic resistance genes. By adding a fluorescent reporter we use Cas13’s collateral cleavage activity to generate a measurable fluorescent signal. This approach will enable clinicians to make rapid, targeted decisions about antibiotic therapies, reducing the reliance on empirical treatments and improving clinical outcomes.

title: TRAPS - Targeted RNA Activated Phase Seperation
text: TRAPS - Targeted RNA Activated Phase Seperation. RNA is a versatile biomolecule functioning as both messenger and catalyst. Understanding its dynamics, localization, and expression in living cells is crucial for decoding cellular function. Existing RNA imaging methods often require fixation or genetic modification and struggle to detect low-abundance RNAs due to poor signal-to-noise ratio. Here, we introduce TRAPS – Targeted RNA Activated Phase Separation, a novel and modular approach for in vivo RNA detection. TRAPS uses catalytically inactive Cas13 fused to GFP-tagged scaffold domains, forming fluorescent condensates upon multivalent RNA binding. This enables simple, real-time visualization and flexible adaption.  Our system allows detection of endogenous RNAs with improved sensitivity and temporal resolution. As proof of concept, we targeted mCherry mRNA in S. cerevisiae. Combined with our software SEASTAR (Side-Effect Aware Sequence Targeting & Ranking) for optimal site selection, TRAPS offers an accessible, versatile platform for RNA studies in living cells and future iGEM applications.

title: PhytoBlock - Let's Save the Future of Chocolate!
text: PhytoBlock - Let's Save the Future of Chocolate!. Black Pod Disease, caused by Phytophthora species, destroys up to 30% of global cocoa yield each year and threatens the livelihoods of farmers. Our project, PhytoBlock, harnesses the natural power of Bacillus subtilis, that is engineered to secrete antimicrobial peptides upon detection of Phytophthora species, hereby preventing Black Pod Disease. By offering an alternative to chemical fungicides, PhytoBlock protects cacao crops, reduces accumulation of chemicals in the environment, and supports long-term agricultural resilience.

title: SPIKY'MUNE- An edible anti-cholera vaccine implemented in cactus
text: SPIKY'MUNE- An edible anti-cholera vaccine implemented in cactus. Each year, cholera causes thousands of deaths in developing countries where access to clean water remains insufficient.
